subsection: 6. Recipe balance, presentation and dishes for different needs

notes.b: A recipe is balanced when a dish or meal supplies the right proportions of nutrients for the people who will eat it. The Department of Health Healthy Eating Guidelines and the Food Pyramid are the checks a cook uses.
points: A balanced main meal usually includes a protein food, a starchy food and vegetables, so that protein, carbohydrate, vitamins, minerals and fibre are all present, with little added fat, sugar and salt.
On the Food Pyramid, vegetables, salad and fruit form the base, because they should be eaten most. Next come wholemeal cereals and breads, potatoes, pasta and rice, then milk, yogurt and cheese.

Higher up are meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts, then a small shelf of fats, spreads and oils, which are used sparingly. Foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt sit at the top and are not needed for health.
Wholegrain or wholemeal versions of starchy foods, and pulses, add fibre, B vitamins and minerals to a dish, so they improve balance.
Oily fish, lean meat, pulses and low-fat dairy supply protein with less saturated fat than fatty cuts of meat and full-fat dairy.

Fresh, frozen or tinned fruit and vegetables in a main course or dessert supply vitamin C, folate and fibre, and extra vegetables add vitamins and minerals. Using less fat, sugar and salt also improves balance.
Balance also covers colour, texture, flavour and cost, so that a meal is appealing as well as affordable.
notes.tip: A balanced main meal usually has a protein food, a starchy food and vegetables. Say 'usually', because meals vary, and don't quote servings-per-day numbers for the pyramid.

notes.b: Modifying (adapting) a recipe means changing its ingredients, quantity or method so that it suits the people eating it. There are six main reasons.
points: To make a dish more nutritious, by adding fibre or reducing fat, sugar or salt, in line with healthy-eating guidelines.
To cater for a person on a special diet, such as a coeliac (someone who cannot eat gluten) who needs gluten-free flour.
To increase or decrease the number of portions, because standard recipes are written for a set number of servings, usually about four adults.
To add variety to a basic recipe, for example by adding nuts to a vegetable stir-fry.
To economise, by substituting an expensive ingredient with a cheaper one, for example margarine for butter in a sponge.
To suit the likes and dislikes of those eating, for example by leaving out an ingredient that a family member avoids.
notes.tip: Questions ask for reasons for modifying a recipe, with an example for each. Give three clear reasons and attach one example to each, such as a coeliac, nuts in a stir-fry or margarine for butter. Don't describe margarine as healthier than butter; it is the cheaper substitute.

notes.h: Methods of modifying a recipe: fat, salt, sugar and fibre
notes.b: Making a dish healthier usually means swapping a few ingredients or changing the cooking method. Each change below targets one nutrient.
points: Reduce fat by grilling, baking, steaming or poaching instead of frying, which adds fat. Also trim visible fat from meat, skim fat from stews, and use a vegetable oil or low-fat spread instead of butter.
Reduce salt by omitting added salt and stock cubes, which are high in salt. Flavour with herbs, spices, garlic or lemon juice instead, and choose reduced-salt products.
Reduce sugar by using less of it, by adding fruit that gives natural sweetness, and by avoiding sugary toppings.

Increase fibre by replacing white flour with wholemeal flour, using brown rice and pasta, and adding oats, pulses and vegetables. Leave the skins on fruit and vegetables, since the skin is a source of fibre.
notes.tip: When asked to adapt a recipe to raise fibre or cut fat, sugar or salt, give specific substitutions, such as wholemeal flour for white or herbs in place of salt, rather than general advice.

notes.h: Methods of modifying a recipe: diets, scaling and flavour
notes.b: Other changes alter who the dish suits or how many it feeds. After any change, the result still has to taste right.
points: Gluten-free cooking replaces wheat flour with a gluten-free flour, such as rice or maize flour, and checks that other ingredients are gluten-free.
Vegetarian versions replace meat with pulses, tofu, eggs or mushrooms, while keeping a source of iron and protein in the dish, because meat is normally where those come from.

Scale a recipe by multiplying or dividing every ingredient by the same factor, so the proportions stay right. Then adjust the tin or dish size and the cooking time, since larger quantities usually take longer, and check the seasoning.
Adapt flavour and texture by substituting herbs and spices, or by using a different fruit or vegetable in season.
Taste and adjust the seasoning after modifying a recipe, because reduced salt or sugar changes the flavour.
notes.tip: For a question on increasing or decreasing portions, say that every ingredient changes by the same factor, then mention tin size, cooking time and seasoning.

notes.b: Aesthetic awareness is a general reaction to how food looks, smells and feels, not a formal test. Sight, smell and texture help a cook judge food before it is bought and while it is prepared.
points: Sight judges appearance, colour, size, shape and surface. Colour and appearance show freshness or ripeness, for example a firm, bright, unbruised apple.
Certain colours are linked to flavours, such as yellow with lemon, and people expect particular appearances: mould is accepted on Stilton cheese but not on bread.
Smell detects aroma through receptor cells in the nasal cavity (the nose), which tell us whether food is fresh or rancid (gone off, as fat does).
Texture is judged by mouth feel and by sight, and a variety of textures, such as a crisp salad served with a soft dish, makes a meal more interesting.
The shape and size of cut pieces affect appearance; uniform cuts look neater and cook evenly.
notes.tip: For a discussion of aesthetic awareness in choosing food, cover sight, smell and texture, each with an example such as yellow with lemon, mould on Stilton but not on bread, or a crisp salad with a soft dish.

notes.h: Aesthetic awareness in preparing and presenting food
notes.b: Food that looks and smells good is more appealing and is eaten with more enjoyment. It also helps appetite, which matters especially for children, older people and the ill, and dishes are judged on presentation.
points: Cut food evenly so it looks neat and cooks evenly. Avoid overcooking, which dulls colour and softens texture; green vegetables cooked briefly in fast-boiling water keep their colour.
A garnish adds colour and contrast, for example parsley on soup, parmesan shavings or grated cheese on pasta, or icing sugar on a sponge or cake.
A garnish should be edible, in keeping with the dish and small enough not to overpower it.
Hot food should be served hot and cold food cold, on warmed plates for hot food and chilled plates for cold food, so the dish stays at its best temperature.
Choose contrasting colours on the plate, such as a red pepper beside green beans, and vary shape and texture.
Arrange food with height and balance, keep the rim of the plate clean and portion each item in proportion to the dish. A neat table setting also adds to the effect.
notes.tip: For the importance of aesthetic awareness, cover colour, garnish and serving temperature in presentation. Make sure any garnish you suggest is edible.

notes.h: Dishes for individuals and family groups
notes.b: The same recipe is not right for everyone. The number of people, their ages and activity levels, and the budget all shape what is cooked.
points: For one person, plan a single-serving dish such as a filled jacket potato, or cook a batch that can be frozen in single portions, which avoids waste.
Someone eating alone, such as an older person or a student, should still make sure the meal supplies enough nutrients.
For a family group, plan meals to suit the ages, tastes, activity levels and budget of the family, use lower-cost cuts and ingredients, and involve the family in choices.
A one-pot or batch dish, such as a casserole, feeds several people at low cost with little washing-up.
Cook a dish in advance and reheat it on a busy day, so that the meal is ready at a convenient time.
Young children need small, soft pieces that are easy to chew, with little added salt and sugar.
Teenagers and active adults need larger portions and energy-rich starchy foods, and teenagers need extra iron and calcium.
Older people often need smaller, nutrient-dense portions (a lot of nutrition in a small amount), with soft textures if chewing is difficult.
notes.tip: For a meal planned for an individual, a family or someone with special needs, name the person's age or need and show how portion size, texture and cooking method suit them.

notes.b: A modified diet changes the choice of food and the cooking methods, but the meal must still be balanced and attractive. For each diet, the cook changes particular ingredients.
points: Coeliac: wheat, barley and rye contain gluten, so gluten-free flours and starches, such as rice and maize, replace them in bread, pastry, sauces and coatings, and labels are checked. Oats must be labelled gluten-free.
Diabetic: carbohydrate portions are controlled and added sugar is reduced, with wholegrain starches and high-fibre vegetables preferred and less fat used.
Low-fat or heart-healthy: lean meat, oily fish and low-fat dairy are used, with grilling, steaming and baking because they need little added fat.
Low-salt: no added salt or stock cubes, processed meats and salted snacks are avoided, and dishes are flavoured with herbs and spices.

Vegetarian and vegan: pulses, tofu, nuts and seeds replace meat, and eggs and dairy foods do so for vegetarians only. Include sources of iron and vitamin B12, use plant-based milks, and check for hidden animal ingredients.
Lactose intolerance: lactose-free milk or a fortified plant alternative replaces milk, and labels are checked for hidden milk ingredients.
High-fibre: wholemeal flour, pulses, vegetables and fruit are used.
notes.tip: Questions on these diets ask how a dish is adapted: name the ingredient you replace and what you replace it with, rather than listing what the person may eat.

keyTerms.definition: A recipe that supplies the right proportions of food groups and nutrients to meet the needs of the people eating it.
The Irish guide to food groups showing how much of each group to eat, from cereals and breads at the base to fats, oils, sugar and salt at the top.
A recipe written for a set number of servings, used as the starting point when adapting quantities.
Adjusting every ingredient in a recipe by the same factor to make more or fewer portions.
Judging the appearance, colour, smell, texture and shape of food when choosing, preparing and serving it.
An edible decoration added to a dish to enhance its appearance and complement its flavour.
Free of the gluten proteins found in wheat, barley and rye, and therefore suitable for a person with coeliac disease.
An eating pattern adapted for a medical condition or a personal choice, such as coeliac, diabetic, vegetarian or low-salt.
A reduced ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, because of too little of the enzyme lactase.
Replacing one ingredient with another to change the nutritional content, cost or suitability of a dish.

questions.prompt: Outline three reasons why a cook might modify a standard recipe.
questions.model: To make the dish more nutritious in line with healthy-eating guidelines, for example by adding fibre or reducing fat, sugar or salt. To cater for an individual on a special diet, such as a coeliac who needs gluten-free flour. To change the number of portions, since standard recipes are written for a set number of servings. To add variety to a basic recipe. To economise by substituting an expensive ingredient with a cheaper one. To suit the likes and dislikes of those eating. Any three with a brief explanation earn full marks.

questions.prompt: Discuss how a cook can adapt a family dish for a family member with coeliac disease so that it stays balanced and appealing.
questions.model: Identify the gluten sources: wheat, barley and rye in flour, bread, pastry, sauces and stock. Replace them with gluten-free flours and starches such as rice or maize flour, and check that stock cubes, sauces and processed ingredients are gluten-free. Keep the balance of the dish: retain a protein food, a starchy food and vegetables, and use wholegrain gluten-free alternatives where available to add fibre, vitamins and minerals. Adjust the method if needed, for example thickening a sauce with a gluten-free starch rather than wheat flour. Presentation: keep the colour contrast and texture variety, add a fresh garnish and serve hot food hot. Avoid cross-contamination by cleaning surfaces and utensils and by using separate equipment for gluten-free cooking. Taste and adjust the seasoning, since the flavour can change when ingredients are substituted. Keep the dish suitable for the rest of the family so that everyone eats the same meal.
